title: Why are nor'easters so windy?
script: Why can a nor'easter feel like a wall of wind? It starts with a strong low-pressure system developing near the U.S. East Coast. Cold air from Canada meets much milder Atlantic air and water near the coast, helping the storm intensify. Air naturally accelerates from areas of higher pressure toward lower pressure. The sharper that pressure changes over distance, the stronger the pressure-gradient force, and the faster the wind can blow. Because Earth is rotating, that moving air curves, so winds spiral counterclockwise around a low-pressure system in the Northern Hemisphere. Ahead of a nor'easter, that circulation often sends powerful winds from the northeast onto the coast — which is where the storm gets its name. A nor'easter is not just a cold-weather hurricane: it is a different kind of cyclone, fueled mainly by strong temperature contrasts and mid-latitude weather systems. So the roaring northeast wind is really the atmosphere trying to balance a big pressure difference.
